newsitem.title: UK: British retail sales growth slows in September.
newsitem.headline: British retail sales growth slows in September.

text.p: Britain's booming retail sales growth slowed to 5.2 percent year-on-year in September but still showed a healthy gain over last year, the British Retail Consortium said on Tuesday.

Sales rose 6.9 percent in August on a like-for-like basis, but the underlying growth rate of 5.8 percent over the past three months compared favourably with three percent growth seen over the same period last year, the BRC said.
It said sales growth was stabilising rather than growing sharply, suggesting fears of a consumer boom were overdone and an early interest rate rise overly hasty.
The BRC said sales were solid across the board but were particularly buoyant in housing-related sectors.
"The level of retail sales increased encouragingly but in a highly competitive market," said Andrew Higginson, chairman of the BRC's economic affairs committee.
"Inflation across retail goods as a whole fell for the third month running. Fears of a runaway consumer boom are misplaced."
The annual rate of inflation in retail goods fell to 2.1 percent in September, the lowest rate of retail goods inflation since the beginning of 1995.
Looking at the breakdown in sales, the BRC noted "a very good month indeed" for furniture and carpets but a fairly poor one for electrical and electronic goods.
The value of food and drink sales increased "satisfactorily" but the clothing and footwear markets remained very competitive.

"Much comment was made last week on the increase in (clothing and footwear) prices from August to September. It should be noted, however, that prices in this sector still remain at below last year's levels," the BRC said.

Retail price figures from the Office for National Statistics showed clothing and footwear prices leapt 5.2 percent in September, the highest jump on record, but were still 0.2 percent lower than they were a year ago.
"The growth or retail sales values now appears to be stabilising, rather than accelerating further, said Andrew Sentance, chief economic advisor to the BRC.
"With little room for tax cuts in the budget (due November 26), it would be premature to push up interest rates to choke off a consumer recovery that has barely started."
